item.title: How to Write Grants for Nonprofits: Federal Proposal Guide
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Learn how to write grants for nonprofits the way federal reviewers score them: needs statement, goals, budget narrative, and Grants.gov submission steps.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To write a federal grant for a nonprofit, start with the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO), not with a template. Find its "Application Review Information" section and write one narrative section for each scored criterion, using the NOFO's own headings. Give each section space in proportion to its points, and make the budget narrative explain every cost. Federal rules require agencies to publish their review criteria and, when the criteria differ in importance, to publish their relative weights. That means the scoring rubric is usually printed in the NOFO you're answering (2 CFR Part 200, Appendix I).

Which option is right for you?

Choose where to start based on how much federal experience you have and how much time or money you can spend. Every path below starts with free official tools.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never applied federallyGet registered first, then read one NOFO's review criteriaSAM.gov (see our SAM.gov status guide)
Small business owner, not a nonprofitCheck eligibility before writing anything, because many NOFOs exclude for-profitsOur small business grant guide
Grant writing is part of your regular jobBuild a reusable outline that matches the eight Appendix I sections2 CFR Appendix I
Researcher applying to NSFWrite to Intellectual Merit and Broader ImpactsNSF merit review
Zero budget, need human helpFree advising from a Small Business Development CenterSBA local assistance
Some budget, want structured trainingA paid proposal-writing courseCandid Learning

What federal reviewers actually score

Reviewers score the criteria printed in the NOFO's "Application Review Information" section, and nothing else. Generic fundraising polish doesn't earn points.

Under the Uniform Guidance, every federal NOFO must use the same or similar section headings, plus a table of contents. The required sections are Basic Information, Eligibility, Program Description, Application Contents and Format, Submission Requirements and Deadlines, Application Review Information, Award Notices, and Post-Award Requirements and Administration (Appendix I). The same appendix says that "if criteria vary in importance, the relative percentages, weights, or other means used to distinguish between them" must be disclosed.

Agencies are also told to make opportunities available "for at least 60 calendar days" and to write them in plain language (2 CFR 200.204). Their Program Description must cover "performance goals, indicators, targets, baseline data, data collection" (Appendix I). This is useful: the NOFO tells you which measures the agency wants you to report.

What scoring looks like in real NOFOs

AgencyScored criteriaNotes
HRSA (HHS)Need, Response, Evaluative Measures, Impact, Resources/Capabilities, Support RequestedIn one HRSA NOFO the weights were 10 / 35 / 15 / 10 / 25 / 5, out of 100 (HRSA-21-066). Weights vary by NOFO.
DOJ / OJPDescription of the need, goals and objectives, project design and implementation, capabilities and competencies, plus the budget"Each section of the proposal narrative and the budget are given a numeric score" (OJP guide)
NSFIntellectual Merit and Broader ImpactsReviewers ask whether the plan is "well-reasoned," whether the team is qualified, and whether resources are adequate (NSF)

The HRSA example shows a common pattern. The needs statement carried only 10 points, while the work plan ("Response") carried 35 and organizational capacity 25. Many first-time applicants spend half their pages on the problem and leave little room for the plan. Size each section to its points.

Since August 2025, Executive Order 14332 has also required senior agency appointees to review new NOFOs, so they line up with agency priorities (EO 14332, govinfo; Ballotpedia summary)). In practice, read the current NOFO's Program Description closely. Don't reuse priority language from an older version of the same program.

How to write each scored section

Write each section as a direct answer to its criterion. Use the NOFO's exact heading and echo its wording so a reviewer can find what they're scoring.

Needs statement (often "Need" or "Statement of the Problem")

The needs statement shows that a specific, measurable problem exists in your service area and that your project addresses it.

  • Open with one local data point and its source, for example a county rate compared with the state rate.
  • Name the population you'll serve and how many people that is.
  • Connect the gap directly to the NOFO's purpose statement, and stop there. You don't get extra points for a long history of the issue.

Example (illustrative): "In [County], [X]% of adults report [condition], compared with [Y]% statewide ([source]). This project will serve [N] residents in [ZIP codes]."

Goals, objectives, and project design (often "Response" or "Project Design and Implementation")

This section usually carries the most points, so it should take up the most space.

  • Write 2–4 objectives that are specific and measurable: who, what, how much, and by when.
  • For each objective, list the activities, the responsible staff role, and the timeline (a table works well).
  • Reuse the NOFO's performance measures word for word as your targets. Appendix I requires agencies to state the indicators and targets they expect (Appendix I).

Capacity (often "Resources/Capabilities" or "Capabilities and Competencies")

Prove that your organization can run this project and manage federal money.

  • Name the key staff, their qualifications, and their percentage of time (it must match the budget).
  • Mention partners and attach signed letters if the NOFO asks for them.
  • Briefly describe your financial controls. NOFOs must describe the agency's risk review factors, so look for them (Appendix I).

Evaluation (often "Evaluative Measures" or "Plan for Collecting Data")

Explain how you'll know the objectives were met: data source, frequency, who collects it, and how results feed back into the program.

Budget narrative (often "Budget Justification" or "Support Requested")

The budget narrative explains how each line item was calculated and why it's needed. OJP, for example, says the budget detail "should provide detailed computation for each budget line item" and "a thorough and clear description of every cost listed." It also says budgets must be "allowable (e.g., reasonable, allocable, and necessary for project activities)" (OJP guide).

Example format (illustrative): "Program Coordinator: $52,000 salary × 50% effort × 12 months = $26,000. Coordinates intake and data collection for Objectives 1–2."

Every person, activity, and number in the narrative should appear in the budget, and every budget line should trace back to an activity in the narrative.

Step-by-step: from NOFO to Grants.gov submission

Register early, build the outline from the NOFO, and submit days before the deadline, not hours.

  1. Register your organization in SAM.gov to get a Unique Entity ID (UEI). Grants.gov says this can take "up to 10 business days" once your documents are ready. Use the same email you'll use at Grants.gov, because that match gives you the expanded AOR role (Grants.gov Quick Start). To check progress, follow our SAM.gov registration status guide.
  2. Create your Grants.gov account. Click Register on the home page, then Get Registered Now. Someone in your organization needs the expanded AOR, standard AOR, or workspace manager role to create a workspace. Only AOR roles can submit (Grants.gov Quick Start).
  3. Download the NOFO and build your outline. Copy the headings from the "Application Contents and Format" and "Application Review Information" sections into a document. Note each criterion's points, the page limit, and the font and format rules.
  4. Create a workspace. Open the opportunity, click Apply, enter an application name, and create the workspace. You need a separate workspace for each application (Grants.gov Quick Start). FEMA's tutorial describes entering the Funding Opportunity number and clicking Create Workspace, then using the Webform link in the Actions column to fill in forms (FEMA Workspace tutorial).
  5. Complete the forms, starting with the SF-424. Attach the project narrative and budget justification as PDFs.
  6. Submit. Click Sign and Submit (FEMA tutorial). Grants.gov says to submit "well before the deadline," and DOJ urges submitting the SF-424 "at least 48 hours prior to the Grants.gov deadline" (Grants.gov; OJP). Some agencies, including DOJ, use a second system after Grants.gov (JustGrants), with its own deadline.
  7. Track the status. Go to Applicants → Check Application Status, then click Search and Details. The statuses move from Received to Validated to Received by Agency to Agency Tracking Number Assigned. "Rejected with Errors" means you have to fix the problem and resubmit (Grants.gov status help).

Common mistakes and fixes

Most problems come from not following the NOFO or from starting registration too late.

MistakeFix
Spending the most pages on the need, even though it carries few pointsSize each section to its points in the NOFO's review criteria
Using your own headingsUse the NOFO's headings word for word so reviewers can find each criterion
Starting SAM.gov registration the week of the deadlineStart now. Registration can take up to 10 business days (Grants.gov)
Different email addresses in SAM.gov and Grants.govUse the same email so expanded AOR is assigned automatically
Budget lines with no mathShow quantity × rate × time for every line (OJP)
Status shows "Rejected with Errors"Read the error email, correct the problem, and resubmit before the deadline (Grants.gov)
Small business applying to a nonprofit-only NOFOCheck the Eligibility section first. See our small business guide

Next steps

You can make real progress today without paying anyone.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Look up your SAM.gov status, or start registering, using our step-by-step SAM.gov guide.
  2. Pick one open NOFO on Grants.gov and copy its review criteria and point values into a blank outline.
  3. Draft your needs statement in one paragraph with one sourced local statistic, then move on to objectives.

If you'd rather get help:

  • SBDC advising (free): SBA-funded Small Business Development Centers offer "free business consulting and low-cost training" (SBA). This suits small businesses and startups. It isn't a grant-writing service, and how much grant expertise you get varies by center.
  • Candid Learning: a free Introduction to Proposal Writing course, plus a three-week Proposal Writing Boot Camp listed at $650 early-bird or $800 regular (as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits nonprofit staff who will write proposals repeatedly. One limitation: it covers proposal writing in general, including foundation proposals, so you still have to apply it to each NOFO's federal rules. If you only need one application, it's probably more than you need.
  • Grants.gov support (free): 1-800-518-4726 or support@grants.gov, available 24/7, for technical submission problems only. They don't help with writing (Grants.gov).

Related guides on Grant Radar:

  • How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step)
  • How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide)

FAQ

What are the main parts of a federal grant proposal?

Most federal proposals include an SF-424 cover form, a project narrative, a budget and budget justification, and attachments. The narrative's sections come from the NOFO, and they usually include need, goals and objectives, project design, capacity, and evaluation (OJP). Always follow the "Application Contents and Format" section of your specific NOFO.

How long does it take to be ready to apply for a federal grant?

Plan for registration before any writing. Grants.gov says SAM.gov registration can take up to 10 business days once your documents are ready (Grants.gov). NOFOs are generally open for at least 60 days (2 CFR 200.204), so starting registration as soon as you spot an opportunity leaves time to write.

How are federal grant applications scored?

Reviewers score each criterion listed in the NOFO's "Application Review Information" section. When the criteria differ in importance, their weights must be disclosed (Appendix I). HRSA, for example, has used a 100-point scale, while NSF uses Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts.

What is a budget narrative in a grant?

A budget narrative (or budget justification) explains how each line item was calculated and why it's necessary for the project. DOJ asks for the calculation and a clear description for every cost (OJP).

Can small businesses apply for the same grants as nonprofits?

Only if the NOFO's Eligibility section lists for-profit organizations. Many federal grants are limited to nonprofits, governments, or institutions. Check eligibility before you write anything.

Sources

  • 2 CFR Part 200, Appendix I – Full Text of Notice of Funding Opportunity (Cornell LII)
  • 2 CFR 200.204 – Notices of funding opportunities (Cornell LII)
  • eCFR: 2 CFR Part 200
  • Grants.gov Quick Start Guide for Applicants
  • Grants.gov – Check Application Status
  • FEMA – Applying Through Grants.gov Workspace (PDF)
  • OJP Grant Application Resource Guide
  • HRSA-21-066 NOFO (PDF)
  • NSF – How We Make Funding Decisions
  • Executive Order 14332 – Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking (govinfo)
  • Ballotpedia – EO: Improving Oversight of Federal Grantmaking)
  • SBA – Small Business Development Centers
  • Candid Learning – Proposal Writing Boot Camp
  • Candid Learning – Live training

item.title: Small Business Grants for Women: Federal Options (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Small business grants for women from the federal government are limited. Learn which SBA programs, SBIR/STTR awards, and WOSB certification apply to you.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

The federal government has no general grant program that gives women money just to start or grow a small business. The SBA says directly: "SBA does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business." The federal options that do exist for women-owned businesses are research grants (SBIR/STTR), set-aside contracts under the Women-Owned Small Business (WOSB) Federal Contract Program, SBA microloans, and free or low-cost help from Women's Business Centers.

Which option is right for you?

Choose based on what your business does today, not on which program sounds most generous.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner or pre-launch, with no funding plan yetA Women's Business Center (free or low-cost counseling)SBA local assistance finder
Tech or science startup with an R&D ideaSBIR/STTR (grants and contracts that don't take equity)SBIR.gov
Business that already sells, or wants to sell, to government agenciesWOSB or EDWOSB certificationSBA Certifications
Small budget and needs under $50,000 for equipment or inventorySBA Microloan (a loan, not a grant)SBA Microloans
Nonprofit that serves women entrepreneursSearch Grants.gov with an eligibility filterGrants.gov Search Grants
Exporter or planning to exportState Trade Expansion Program (STEP) through your stateSBA Grants page

Why each pick:

  • Women's Business Center: the counseling is "free, to low-cost," so you can start without spending anything.
  • SBIR/STTR: this is the largest real federal grant source open to for-profit small businesses. It is only for R&D work.
  • WOSB: it limits competition for some federal contracts, which turns into revenue rather than a one-time grant.
  • Microloan: it is fast, small, and meant for early-stage needs. You have to repay it.

What federal funding actually exists for women-owned businesses

Federal money for women business owners comes through four channels, and only one of them is a true business grant.

SBIR and STTR research grants

SBIR and STTR fund research and development at small businesses. They pay "equity free funding through federal agencies" across 11 participating agencies. As of October 2026, SBIR.gov lists Phase I awards of up to $335,937 and Phase II awards of up to $2,239,578 (SBIR.gov). Each agency sets its own amounts and topics, so check every solicitation.

Status matters here. Both programs lapsed on September 30, 2025, and new awards paused. They were reauthorized on April 13, 2026, under the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act of 2026 (S. 3971), which runs through September 30, 2031 (Crowell & Moring; IEDC). Starting in fiscal year 2027, agencies will set their own caps on how many proposals one company can submit (Crowell & Moring).

Not for: service, retail, or restaurant businesses with no research component. Limitation: competition is strong, and the work has to match a topic an agency has published.

WOSB Federal Contract Program (contracts, not grants)

The WOSB program limits competition for certain federal contracts to certified women-owned firms. The government's goal is to award 5% of federal contracting dollars to these businesses (SBA).

Eligibility (SBA; 13 CFR Part 127):

  • The business is small under SBA size standards.
  • It is at least 51% owned and controlled by women who are U.S. citizens.
  • Women manage day-to-day operations and make long-term decisions.
  • EDWOSB (economically disadvantaged) has extra limits for each qualifying owner: personal net worth under $850,000, adjusted gross income of $400,000 or less averaged over three years, and personal assets of $6.5 million or less.

Not for: businesses that don't want to sell to government agencies. Limitation: certification doesn't guarantee any contract. You still have to find and win bids.

SBA Microloans (loan, not grant)

Microloans go up to $50,000 and average about $13,000. Terms run up to seven years, and interest rates are generally 8% to 13%, depending on the intermediary lender (as of October 2026; check the official page) (SBA). You can use the money for working capital, inventory, supplies, and equipment. You can't use it to pay existing debts or buy real estate.

Not for: anyone who needs money they don't have to repay.

Women's Business Centers and other SBA-funded help

SBA grants go to organizations that train entrepreneurs, and those organizations pass the help on to you. Women's Business Centers offer free or low-cost counseling and training. The SBA also funds the Women Veteran Entrepreneurship Training Program for women veterans, service members, and spouses (SBA Grants).

How to find and apply for a federal grant, step by step

You'll register once and then search on Grants.gov or SBIR.gov. Most federal awards require an active SAM.gov registration.

Step 1: Register your entity in SAM.gov

  1. Go to SAM.gov, sign in through Login.gov, and start the entity registration.
  2. Use your legal business name and address exactly as they appear in IRS records.
  3. Renew every 365 days. SAM.gov states: "You must renew your registration every 365 days to keep it active."

If you're already registered, confirm you're active with our guide to checking your SAM.gov registration status.

Step 2: Search Grants.gov with the right filters

  1. Open Grants.gov → Search Grants.
  2. Under Opportunity Status, check Posted, and also Forecasted if you want to see upcoming programs.
  3. Under Eligibility, change All Eligibilities to the category that fits you, such as small businesses or nonprofits.
  4. In Keyword(s), try "women," "entrepreneur," or your industry.
  5. Set the sort to Close Date (Ascending) so the nearest deadlines show first.

Step 3: For R&D, check SBIR.gov solicitations

Open SBIR.gov, filter open topics by agency, and read the agency's own solicitation for page limits and amounts. Rules for FY2027 may change because of the new submission caps (Crowell & Moring).

Step 4: For WOSB, apply through SBA Certifications

  1. Confirm your primary NAICS code and your size standard.
  2. Make sure your SAM.gov profile is active.
  3. Go to SBA Certifications, use the pre-application checklists, and upload your documents, including proof of citizenship (SBA).
  4. Update your SAM.gov profile every year. SBA does a program examination every three years.

You can also get certified through an SBA-approved third-party certifier: the El Paso Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, the National Women Business Owners Corporation, the U.S. Women's Chamber of Commerce, or the Women's Business Enterprise National Council. These certifiers may charge fees (SBA).

For a fuller walkthrough of application packages, see How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide).

Common mistakes and how to fix them

Most rejections and delays come from eligibility mismatches and paperwork problems, not from weak ideas.

MistakeFix
Applying to "grant" sites that ask for a feeFederal grants are listed on Grants.gov and SBIR.gov. Start your search there.
Assuming SBA gives grants to start a businessIt doesn't (SBA). Look at microloans, SBIR, or WOSB instead.
Letting SAM.gov expire mid-applicationRenew before the 365-day mark (SAM.gov).
Claiming WOSB when a man controls key decisionsWomen must control both daily operations and long-term decisions (13 CFR 127).
Filtering Grants.gov only by keywordAdd the Eligibility filter. Many results only accept states, universities, or nonprofits.
Pitching a product with no R&D to SBIRSBIR funds research that meets an agency's goals, not general growth (SBA).

What nonprofits and researchers should know

For nonprofits, the federal money aimed at women entrepreneurs usually goes to organizations that serve them, not to the business owners themselves. The SBA funds counseling and training organizations rather than individual businesses. That includes Women's Business Centers, PRIME (Program for Investors in Microentrepreneurs), SCORE, and SBDCs (SBA Grants). If your nonprofit runs or wants to run this kind of program, use the Eligibility filter on Grants.gov to find nonprofit opportunities and watch for SBA notices of funding opportunity. Our federal proposal guide for nonprofits covers narratives, budgets, and evaluation sections.

Researchers at universities usually take part in STTR by partnering with a small business. In STTR, the small business is the applicant (SBIR.gov).

Next steps

You can make real progress today without paying anyone.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Check or start your SAM.gov registration (SAM.gov).
  2. Run one Grants.gov search with Posted and Forecasted checked and the Eligibility filter set to your category.
  3. If you sell to government agencies, open SBA Certifications and read the WOSB checklist to see whether you qualify.

If you'd rather not do it alone:

  • Women's Business Center (free to low-cost): good for first-time applicants who want help with a business plan or loan package. It's less useful if you need deep technical help writing an SBIR proposal. Counseling availability depends on the local center (SBA).
  • SBA-approved third-party WOSB certifiers (fees vary; as of October 2026, check each certifier's official page): good if you also want a private-sector women-owned certification. It's not needed if you only want federal WOSB status, because you can apply directly through SBA Certifications (SBA).
  • SBDCs and SCORE (SBA resource partners): good for general business and finance mentoring. They're less specialized than a paid proposal consultant for complex R&D bids (SBA Grants).

Related guides on Grant Radar:

  • How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step)
  • How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide)
  • How to Write Grants for Nonprofits: Federal Proposal Guide

FAQ

Does the federal government give free grants to women to start a business?

No, not as a general program. The SBA states that it does not give grants to start or expand a business (SBA). Federal options include SBIR/STTR for R&D, WOSB contracting, and microloans.

Are SBIR grants available again in 2026?

Yes. SBIR and STTR were reauthorized on April 13, 2026, through September 30, 2031, after a six-month lapse (Crowell & Moring). Check each agency's solicitation for its current open topics.

What is the difference between WOSB and EDWOSB?

Both require at least 51% ownership and control by women who are U.S. citizens. EDWOSB adds economic limits for each owner: net worth under $850,000, average AGI of $400,000 or less, and personal assets of $6.5 million or less (SBA).

How much can I borrow with an SBA microloan?

Up to $50,000, with an average of about $13,000 and terms of up to seven years (SBA). Rates generally run 8% to 13%, depending on the lender.

Is it safe to pay a website to find women's business grants?

You don't need to. Federal grant listings are public on Grants.gov and SBIR.gov. Be careful with any service that promises a guaranteed grant.

Sources

  • SBA – Grants
  • SBA – Women-Owned Small Business Federal Contract Program
  • eCFR – 13 CFR Part 127
  • SBA – Women's Business Centers
  • SBA – Microloans
  • SBA Certifications portal
  • SBIR.gov – About
  • Grants.gov – Search Grants
  • SAM.gov – Entity Registration
  • Crowell & Moring – SBIR/STTR Programs Reauthorized After Six-Month Lapse
  • IEDC – Congress Reauthorizes SBIR and STTR

Originally published at Outlay.

item.title: How to Apply for Grants for Small Business (2026 Guide)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How to apply for grants for small business in 2026: set up SAM.gov, get your UEI, register on Grants.gov, filter by eligibility, and submit before the deadline.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To apply for a federal grant as a small business, do the steps in this order: register your entity on SAM.gov, which gives you a Unique Entity ID (UEI); create a Grants.gov account and add an organization profile using that UEI; then search for open opportunities with the Eligibility filter set to your applicant type and submit through a Workspace. Each step depends on the one before it. SAM.gov can take 7–10 business days to process, so start now, even before you've picked a grant. Also check your expectations: the SBA says it "does not provide grants for starting and expanding a business". Most federal grants go to specific purposes, such as research (SBIR/STTR), exporting or nonprofit programs.

Which option is right for you?

Your applicant type decides your first move, so find your row below before you open any website.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
First-time applicant, for-profit small businessFull SAM.gov entity registration for financial assistanceSAM.gov Entity Registration
Tech or research startupSBIR/STTR (research and development funding that doesn't take equity)SBIR.gov
Nonprofit / 501(c)(3)SAM.gov registration, then Grants.gov organization profileGrants.gov Applicant Registration
Individual researcher or artist (no company)Grants.gov individual profile, for "Individuals" opportunities onlyGrants.gov Grant Eligibility
Already registered and applying regularlyCheck that your SAM.gov registration is active, then use Grants.gov WorkspaceCheck SAM.gov status
Small business that wants to exportYour state's STEP program (SBA funds the states, not individual companies)SBA Grants page
No budget for helpFree registration help from an APEX Accelerator or the Federal Service DeskGSA scam warning and free help

One-line reasons:

  • Beginner business: you need full registration, not just a UEI, before you can apply for any federal award.
  • Startup doing research: SBIR/STTR is the main federal grant path written for for-profit small businesses.
  • On a budget: registration costs nothing, and anyone asking you to pay for it is not the government.

What federal grants actually exist for small businesses?

Federal grants for small businesses are narrow and tied to a specific purpose. They are not general startup money.

The SBA lists these as its main grant programs (SBA):

  • SBIR and STTR: research and development funding for work that could become a product.
  • STEP (State Trade Expansion Program): money goes to state and territory governments, which then help established small businesses export.
  • Empower to Grow (E2G) Manufacturing grant: applications were closed when the SBA page was checked.
  • Grants to organizations that support veteran-owned businesses, Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) and microenterprise lenders (PRIME).

SBIR/STTR deserves a closer look. Its legal authority lapsed on October 1, 2025, and the program was reauthorized on April 13, 2026 through September 30, 2031. SBIR.gov says 11 federal agencies take part. As of April 2026, Phase I awards go up to $323,090 and Phase II awards up to $2,153,927 (SBIR.gov). The reauthorization also adds proposal submission limits, which agencies will phase in during later funding cycles (IEDC). Check each solicitation for its current cap.

Who SBIR is not for: a business with no research or development work, such as a typical retail shop or service firm. Those businesses will usually do better with state or local programs, or with loans.

Step 1: Register your entity on SAM.gov and get your UEI

To apply for a federal award, you need a full entity registration on SAM.gov. A UEI on its own is not enough.

SAM.gov offers two paths. "Get a Unique Entity ID" only asks for your legal business name and physical address. However, it does not let you apply for federal awards directly. It is meant for sub-awardees and similar cases (SAM.gov). First-time applicants often pick this shortcut by mistake.

Gather these before you start (from the SAM.gov Entity Registration Checklist):

  • EIN/TIN, with your legal name exactly as the IRS has it
  • Bank account details for receiving payments
  • NAICS code (the industry classification code for your business)
  • Points of contact (POCs)

Steps:

  1. Go to SAM.gov and click Sign In in the upper right. Accept the terms. If you don't have an account, create one through Login.gov (DOL quick start guide).
  2. In your Workspace, find the Entities widget and click Get Started.
  3. Choose Register Entity, not "Get a Unique Entity ID" (SAM.gov).
  4. Enter the information you gathered. Name an Electronic Business Point of Contact (EBiz POC): this person will control Grants.gov access later (Grants.gov).
  5. Submit, then wait. Allow up to 10 business days for the registration to become active. If something can't be verified, it "could take weeks or months" (Grants.gov).

Key facts:

  • Registration is free.
  • You must renew every 365 days (SAM.gov).
  • To confirm your registration went through, use our guide: How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step).

Step 2: Create your Grants.gov account and organization profile

Once SAM.gov shows your registration as active, set up Grants.gov and link it to your UEI.

Grants.gov says it can take 24–48 hours after SAM activation for your data to appear there. If Grants.gov doesn't recognize your UEI, wait a day before you contact support.

  1. On Grants.gov, click Register in the top banner and follow the on-screen instructions. This step is usually done the same day (Grants.gov).
  2. The EBiz POC should create the account with the same email address used in SAM.gov (Grants.gov).
  3. Add an organization applicant profile and enter your UEI. Each profile represents one applicant organization (Grants.gov FAQs).
  4. The EBiz POC assigns roles to the people who will work on applications. The main roles are:
  5. Authorized Organization Representative (AOR): the person who can submit applications for the organization.
  6. Workspace Manager: the person who can manage application Workspaces.

To check who has which role, open My Account and go to the Manage Profiles tab (Grants.gov).

Individuals can register with an individual profile. However, with that profile you can only apply to opportunities open to individuals, and "most of the funding opportunities on Grants.gov are for organizations" (Grants.gov).

Step 3: Find grants you're actually eligible for

To avoid wasted applications, filter by eligibility first. Leave keywords for later.

Grants.gov Search Grants has these filters (Grants.gov):

  • Opportunity Status: Forecasted, Posted, Closed, Archived
  • Funding Instrument Type
  • Eligibility
  • Category
  • Agency

Grants.gov eligibility types include government, education, public housing, nonprofit (501(c)(3) and non-501(c)(3)), for-profit organizations other than small businesses, small businesses, and individuals. A "small business" is defined by SBA size standards for your industry (Grants.gov).

A practical filter sequence:

  1. Set Opportunity Status to Posted. Add Forecasted if you want to see grants coming later.
  2. Under Eligibility, check only your applicant type, for example "Small businesses."
  3. Narrow down by Category or Agency.
  4. Open the funding notice (NOFO) for each result. Read the eligibility, cost-sharing and deadline sections before anything else.

Example: if a nonprofit filters only by keyword, such as "workforce," the results can include grants open only to state governments. Adding the Eligibility filter removes those before you spend time reading them.

Simpler.Grants.gov is a newer search interface for the same opportunities. It's useful for browsing. Before you apply, still confirm the instructions in the official notice.

Step 4: Apply in Workspace and submit early

Fill out the application in a Grants.gov Workspace and submit it 24–48 hours before the deadline.

  1. From the opportunity page, start a Workspace (a shared online folder for one application) and add your team members.
  2. Complete the forms. Most include the SF-424, the standard federal application form (SF-424 instructions). Upload attachments in the format the notice asks for.
  3. An AOR submits the application. Grants.gov recommends submitting at least 24–48 hours before the close date, and validation can take up to two business days.
  4. Watch your inbox for two emails: a submission receipt, then either a validation email or a rejection email listing errors. If neither arrives, check your spam folder and contact support@grants.gov (Grants.gov Help).
  5. Track progress on Track My Application until the status says "Agency Tracking Number Assigned" (Grants.gov FAQs).

Common mistakes and fixes

Almost all first-time blockers come from doing the steps out of order, or from a mismatch between your SAM.gov record and your other records.

MistakeFix
Got a "UEI only" and tried to applyGo back to SAM.gov and complete Register Entity (SAM.gov)
Started SAM.gov a week before the deadlineStart registration 3–4+ weeks ahead. Verification issues can take weeks (Grants.gov)
Legal name or address doesn't match IRS recordsEnter your name and address exactly as the IRS has them. New EINs may need time before they match (SAM checklist)
Nobody has the AOR roleThe EBiz POC assigns it under Manage Profiles (Grants.gov)
SAM.gov registration expiredRenew every 365 days (SAM.gov)
Paid a "SAM registration service"Registration is always free. Treat payment requests as possible fraud (GSA)
Submitted 10 minutes before the deadlineSubmit 24–48 hours early to leave time to fix errors

Next steps

You can finish the setup work today and have your registration processing before you even choose a grant.

Do these today:

  1. Gather your EIN, bank details, NAICS code and the name of your EBiz POC. Then start Register Entity on SAM.gov.
  2. Create your Login.gov account and Grants.gov account so they're ready when SAM.gov activates.
  3. Save a Grants.gov search with Posted + Forecasted status and your eligibility type, and check it weekly.

If you'd rather not do it yourself (costs as of October 2026; check the official pages):

  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs): free. They help with SAM.gov registration and work out of 300+ locations.
  • Good fit: businesses that also want to sell to the government under contract.
  • Limitation: they focus on contracting, so they're less specialized in writing grant proposals.
  • Federal Service Desk: free help with SAM.gov problems (GSA).
  • Limitation: it fixes registration issues only and gives no strategy advice.
  • Small Business Development Centers: individual advising on planning and access to capital (SBA).
  • Good fit: owners still deciding whether a grant fits their business at all.
  • Limitation: cost and grant expertise vary by center, so ask your local center first.
  • Paid grant writers or consultants: prices vary widely, so get a written quote.
  • Good fit: SBIR applicants or nonprofits facing complex federal notices.
  • Not for: anyone who hasn't finished SAM.gov yet. Do the free registration first.

Related guide on this site: How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step)

FAQ

Can I get a federal grant to start a small business?

Usually not. The SBA says it does not provide grants for starting or expanding a business (SBA). Federal grants for for-profit companies mostly fund research (SBIR/STTR) or specific public goals. Start-up money more often comes from loans, state or local programs, or investors.

How long does it take to be ready to apply?

Plan on about 2–4 weeks. SAM.gov takes 7–10 business days, or longer if your details need extra verification, and Grants.gov needs 24–48 hours after that to sync (Grants.gov). Your Grants.gov account itself is usually set up the same day.

Is the UEI the same as SAM.gov registration?

No. You can get a UEI with only your name and address, but that does not let you apply for federal awards directly. To apply, you need a full entity registration (SAM.gov).

Do I have to pay to register on SAM.gov or Grants.gov?

No. SAM.gov registration, updates and renewals are free, and the government will never ask you to pay for them (GSA).

Can I apply as an individual without a company?

Yes, but only for opportunities open to "Individuals." Most Grants.gov opportunities are for organizations (Grants.gov).

item.title: How to Check SAM.gov Registration Status (Step by Step)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Learn how to check SAM.gov registration status in Workspace or the public entity search, what Active, Inactive and Submitted mean, and what to do next.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

You can check your SAM.gov registration status in two ways. If you have a role in the entity, sign in to SAM.gov, open Workspace and look at your entity's status and expiration date. If you don't, use the public Search → Entity Information lookup with your UEI or legal business name. You can only receive a federal grant if the status reads Active Registration. Every other status, including Inactive (expired), Work in Progress and Submitted (in review), means you can't get an award yet (EXIM; 2 CFR 25.200).

Which option is right for you?

Use the signed-in Workspace view if you manage the registration, and the public search if you only need a quick look.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner or first-time applicant who just submitted a registrationCheck Entity Status tool (sign-in required). It shows where a new submission is in processingSAM.gov home → Check Registration Status (GSA bulletin)
Entity Administrator or grants staff checking before each deadline (daily work use)Workspace dashboard. It shows status, expiration date and the Renew Entity actionSAM.gov → Sign In → Workspace (EXIM)
No SAM.gov login, or checking a partner or subrecipientPublic entity search. No account needed, but private records won't appearSAM.gov → Search → Entity Information (GovCon in a Box)
Tight budget and you're stuckFree help from the Federal Service Desk or an APEX AcceleratorFSD.gov or APEX Accelerators

One-line reasons:

  • Beginner: Check Entity Status shows pre-active stages like Submitted that the public search may not.
  • Daily use: Workspace is the only place where you can see the expiration date and renew in the same screen.
  • Budget: SAM.gov registration is "always free," so you never have to pay to check or renew (GSA).

Method 1: Check status in your SAM.gov Workspace (signed in)

If you're an Entity Administrator or have another role in the entity, Workspace is the most complete view. Here's how to use it.

Step-by-step

  1. Go to SAM.gov and select Sign In (top right). SAM.gov sign-in goes through Login.gov, so have your Login.gov credentials and two-factor device ready.
  2. In the top menu bar, select Workspace. It sits next to Sign Out (GovCon in a Box).
  3. Find the Entity Management area. Your entities are counted in status bubbles. For example, a "1" next to Active means one active registration. Select the bubble that shows a number (EXIM).
  4. In the entity list, read three things for your entity:
  5. Status (for example, Active Registration, Work in Progress Registration, Submitted Registration)
  6. UEI (a 12-character alphanumeric ID, per the DOJ)
  7. Expiration date
  8. If the expiration date is close, open the entity's action menu and choose Renew Entity. Renewing means you have to log in and actively submit. It does not happen automatically (EXIM).

What this screen tells you that the FAQ pages don't

The status bubbles group your entities by stage, so you can see right away whether something is stuck in Work in Progress (you still owe information) or in Submitted (you're waiting on validation). A grants administrator who manages several entities, such as a university with affiliated organizations, can spot a lapsed one in seconds this way.

Method 2: Use the Check Entity Status tool (best right after submitting)

The Check Entity Status tool is the official way to track a registration you just submitted or a UEI request that's still pending (GSA bulletin, Dec 2022).

Step-by-step

  1. Sign in to SAM.gov.
  2. On the home page, select Check Registration Status (also labeled Check Entity Status).
  3. Enter one of the following:
  4. Unique Entity ID or CAGE code, if you have a registration, or
  5. your legal business name, if you only have a UEI assigned or are still getting one (GSA bulletin).
  6. Read the status shown and compare it with the table in the next section.

Limitation: "Unless you are a federal government user, you must have a role assigned by an entity" to use this tool (GSA bulletin). If a consultant or former employee set up the registration, ask the current Entity Administrator to give you a role first.

Method 3: Public entity search (no login)

The public search works without an account and shows registration status and expiration date for any entity whose record is public (GovCon in a Box).

  1. Go to SAM.gov and select Search in the top menu.
  2. Choose the Entity Information domain.
  3. Enter the UEI or legal business name and run the search.
  4. Open the result to see the status and expiration date.

Who this is not for: anyone tracking a registration that isn't active yet, and entities that have set their record to private. Private records won't appear in public search (Business2Government). Public records also leave out sensitive data such as banking details and Tax ID.

What each SAM.gov status means for grant eligibility

Only Active Registration lets you apply through Grants.gov and receive an award. Federal rules require you to stay active the whole time an application is under consideration or an award is open (2 CFR 25.200).

Status on screenWhat it means (official definition, via EXIM)Grant eligible?What to do
Active RegistrationUEI assigned and registration complete. Expires one year after submissionYesNote the expiration date and set a reminder 60 days before
Inactive Registration (what most people call "expired")There was an active registration, but it expiredNoRenew now. Expect up to 10 business days to reactivate
Submitted Registration (the "in review" stage)All required information entered; final validations in progressNot yetWait. Watch your email and don't edit unless asked
Work in Progress RegistrationStarted, but more information is neededNoOpen the registration and finish the missing sections
ID AssignedYou have a UEI, but no full registration was startedDepends on the program. Many grants need a full registrationCheck the funding notice. Start a full registration if it requires one
Pending ID AssignmentIn Entity Validation; a Federal Service Desk incident is under reviewNoRespond to any FSD request for documents

A note on terms: SAM.gov doesn't use the words "Expired" or "In Review" as status labels. Those everyday terms match Inactive Registration and Submitted Registration (or Pending ID Assignment if your entity is stuck in validation) (EXIM).

Why "Active" on SAM.gov isn't always enough on the same day

Grants.gov says that once your SAM registration is active, it can take 24–48 hours before that information reaches Grants.gov and you can submit (Grants.gov help). Agency systems can add more time. NSF, for example, takes up to two business days to receive new SAM data (NSF SBIR). For example, if your registration turns Active the morning of a deadline, you could still miss that deadline.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

Most status problems come from timing, access or contact details, not from the registration itself.

  • Waiting until deadline week to renew. The DOJ advises starting registration or renewal 30 days before any deadline (DOJ JustGrants). Processing can take up to 10 business days (Grants.gov quick start), and NSF warns that it can take up to a month (NSF SBIR).
  • Ignoring renewal emails. SAM.gov sends reminders 60, 30 and 15 days before expiration (EXIM). They always come from a .gov address (GSA). If a reminder went to a former employee, add a current administrator.
  • Assuming the renewal happened automatically. Nothing renews until someone selects Renew Entity and submits (EXIM).
  • Mismatched emails between systems. Grants.gov asks you to use the same email for your SAM.gov electronic business point of contact and your Grants.gov registration (Grants.gov quick start).
  • Paying for a "renewal" email you didn't expect. Registration in SAM.gov is always free. Messages that demand payment don't come from the government (GSA; BBB).
  • Getting "no results" in public search. Your record may be private or not active yet. Sign in and use Workspace or Check Entity Status instead.

Next steps

The fastest way to protect your eligibility is to confirm your status today and put the expiration date on your calendar.

1. Do it yourself today

  • Sign in, open Workspace, and write down your status, UEI and expiration date.
  • If the expiration date is within 60 days, select Renew Entity now. Don't wait for the last reminder.
  • Make sure at least two current staff members hold roles in the entity, so renewal emails and access don't depend on one person.

2. If you'd rather not do it yourself

  • Federal Service Desk (FSD.gov) costs nothing and answers SAM.gov questions directly. Suits: anyone with a specific error or a stuck validation. Not for: people who want someone else to do the work. FSD guides you but won't complete the registration for you.
  • APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) give free, hands-on help with SAM.gov registration through local offices across the U.S. (SBIR.gov; NM APEX example). Suits: small businesses, especially those also thinking about federal contracts. Limitation: they focus on government contracting, so a grant-only nonprofit or individual researcher should ask the local office whether they serve their case. Wait times vary by office.
  • Paid registration services or grant consultants charge fees that vary by provider (as of October 2026; check the provider's official page). Suits: organizations with no staff time and complex ownership structures. Not for: anyone on a tight budget. GSA points out that paid help is never required, and some services are misleading (GSA). If you hire one, keep your organization as Entity Administrator.

3. Related guides on Grant Radar Grant Radar doesn't have related guides on UEI setup, Grants.gov registration or renewal checklists yet. Check the Grant Radar home page for new guides as they're published.

FAQ

How long does it take for SAM.gov registration to become active?

Grants.gov says to allow up to 10 business days if your documents (validated address, Tax ID) are in order (Grants.gov). NSF notes that it can take up to a month when information is incomplete (NSF SBIR). Add 24–48 hours after activation before Grants.gov recognizes it (Grants.gov help).

Can I check SAM.gov registration status without logging in?

Yes. Use Search → Entity Information and enter the UEI or business name. Records set to private won't appear, and a registration that isn't active yet may not show up either, so sign in and use Workspace in those cases.

How often do I need to renew my SAM.gov registration?

Every year. Registrations expire one year after submission, and federal rules require you to review and update your information annually (EXIM; 2 CFR 25.200). Renewal reminders arrive 60, 30 and 15 days before expiration.

Can I apply for a grant if my SAM.gov status is "Submitted"?

You can prepare your application, but you can't submit it through Grants.gov until all registration steps are complete and the status is Active (Grants.gov help). Check your funding notice too, because some agencies set their own registration deadlines.

What happens if my SAM.gov registration expires during an open award?

Your status changes to Inactive, and you no longer meet the rule to stay active while you hold an award (2 CFR 25.200). For example, NSF says it will block award approval actions if a registration isn't revalidated (NSF SBIR). Renew right away and tell your program officer.
